stem: A sine wave of wavelength '\(\lambda\)' is travelling in a medium. What is the minimum distance between two particles of the medium which always have the same speed?
solution:
**(B)** \(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\)

For a progressive wave \(y = A\sin(kx - \omega t)\), the particle velocity is \(v_p = -A\omega\cos(kx - \omega t)\).

Two particles at \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) have the same SPEED at every instant when \(|\cos(kx_1 - \omega t)| = |\cos(kx_2 - \omega t)|\) for all \(t\), which requires \(k(x_2 - x_1) = n\pi\), i.e. \(x_2 - x_1 = \dfrac{n\lambda}{2}\).

The smallest such separation is \(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\).

Particles \(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\) apart are in antiphase, so their velocities are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, and their SPEEDS are therefore equal. Particles a full \(\lambda\) apart also have equal speeds, but that separation is not the minimum.

\(\therefore\) minimum distance \(= \dfrac{\lambda}{2}\)

subtopic: Vibrations of a Stretched String and Sonometer
stem: Velocity of a transverse wave along a stretched string is proportional to ________. (\(T\) = tension in the string)
solution:
**(A)** \(\sqrt{T}\)

The speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string is

\(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{m}}\)

where \(m\) is the mass per unit length. With \(m\) fixed, \(v \propto \sqrt{T}\).

stem: The equation of a simple harmonic progressive wave travelling on a string is \(y = 8\ sin(0.02x - 4t)\text{ cm}\). The speed of the wave is ________.
solution:
**(D)** \(200\text{ cm/s}\)

Comparing \(y = 8\sin(0.02x - 4t)\) with \(y = A\sin(kx - \omega t)\):

\(k = 0.02\text{ cm}^{-1}\), \(\omega = 4\text{ rad/s}\)

\(\therefore v = \dfrac{\omega}{k} = \dfrac{4}{0.02} = 200\text{ cm/s}\)

Cross-check: \(\lambda = \dfrac{2\pi}{k} = 314.16\text{ cm}\) and \(n = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi} = 0.6366\text{ Hz}\), so \(n\lambda = 200\text{ cm/s}\).

stem: If sound waves are reflected from surface of denser medium, there is phase change of ________.
solution:
**(D)** \(\pi\) rad

When a wave is reflected from the surface of a denser medium (a rigid boundary), the reflected wave suffers a phase change of \(\pi\) radian — a crest returns as a trough.

Reflection from a rarer medium (a free boundary) produces no phase change.

This \(\pi\) phase reversal at a rigid boundary is what makes the boundary a NODE when the incident and reflected waves superpose to form a stationary wave.

stem: Explain the reflection of transverse and longitudinal waves from a denser medium and rarer medium.
solution:
**Reflection from a DENSER medium (rigid boundary)**

The boundary cannot move, so the reflected wave must cancel the incident displacement there.

- Transverse wave: the reflected wave suffers a phase change of \(\pi\) radian. A crest is reflected as a trough and a trough as a crest.
- Longitudinal wave: a compression is reflected as a compression and a rarefaction as a rarefaction. The DISPLACEMENT wave undergoes a \(\pi\) phase change (the boundary is a displacement node), while the pressure wave does not.

**Reflection from a RARER medium (free boundary)**

The boundary is free to move, so the displacement there is a maximum.

- Transverse wave: there is NO phase change. A crest is reflected as a crest.
- Longitudinal wave: a compression is reflected as a rarefaction and a rarefaction as a compression. The displacement wave suffers no phase change (the boundary is a displacement antinode), while the pressure wave undergoes a \(\pi\) change.

In both cases the reflected wave has the same speed, frequency and wavelength as the incident wave, since it travels in the same medium.

stem: Explain Doppler effect in sound. State any two applications of Doppler effect.
solution:
**Doppler effect in sound**

The Doppler effect is the apparent change in the frequency of sound heard by a listener when there is relative motion between the source of sound and the listener. The frequency actually emitted by the source does not change; only the frequency received by the listener does.

When the source and the listener approach each other, the apparent frequency is greater than the true frequency. When they recede from each other, the apparent frequency is smaller.

If \(n\) is the frequency of the source, \(v\) the speed of sound in air, \(v_L\) the speed of the listener and \(v_S\) the speed of the source, both measured along the line joining them, then the apparent frequency is

\(n_{a} = n\left(\dfrac{v \pm v_L}{v \mp v_S}\right)\)

the upper signs being taken when the motion is towards the other body.

**Applications of the Doppler effect**

1. **RADAR speed measurement.** The frequency of a wave reflected from a moving vehicle is shifted, and the shift gives the speed of the vehicle.
2. **Medical diagnosis (Doppler sonography).** The shift in the frequency of ultrasound reflected from flowing blood or from a beating heart gives the speed of the flow.

stem: In stationary wave, the distance between a node and its adjacent antinode is ________.
solution:
**(B)** \(\dfrac{\lambda}{4}\)

In a stationary wave, consecutive nodes are \(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\) apart and an antinode lies midway between two nodes.

Hence the distance between a node and the antinode adjacent to it is \(\dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{\lambda}{2} = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}\).

stem: Phase difference between a node and an adjacent antinode in a stationary wave is _____.
solution:
**(B)** \(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\)

A node and the antinode next to it are separated by \(\Delta x = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}\). Converting that path difference to a phase difference,

\(\Delta \phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \times \Delta x = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda} \times \dfrac{\lambda}{4} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\)

The convention used here is the progressive-wave relation between path difference and phase difference. Read strictly as \(y = 2A\sin(kx)\cos(\omega t)\), every particle within one loop of a stationary wave shares the same time-phase \(\cos(\omega t)\), which would make the phase difference \(0\), and a node does not oscillate at all. As \(0\) is not among the given alternatives, the intended relation is \(\Delta\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x\).

stem: A standing wave is produced on a string fixed at one end and free at other. The length of string must be an ________.
solution:
**(A)** odd integral multiple of \(\dfrac{\lambda}{4}\)

The fixed end must be a node and the free end must be an antinode.

The distance from a node to the adjacent antinode is \(\dfrac{\lambda}{4}\), and each further loop adds \(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\). Hence

\(L = \dfrac{\lambda}{4} + p\,\dfrac{\lambda}{2} = (2p + 1)\dfrac{\lambda}{4}\), where \(p = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\)

So \(L\) is an ODD integral multiple of \(\dfrac{\lambda}{4}\). A string fixed at BOTH ends would instead have a node at each end, giving lengths that are integral multiples of \(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\).

stem: A string of length 2 m is vibrating with 2 loops. The distance between its node and adjacent antinode is _____.
solution:
**(A)** \(0.5\) m

Each loop of a stationary wave is \(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\) long. With 2 loops in a length of 2 m,

\(L = 2 \times \dfrac{\lambda}{2} = \lambda\), so \(\lambda = 2\text{ m}\)

The distance between a node and the adjacent antinode is

\(\therefore \dfrac{\lambda}{4} = \dfrac{2}{4} = 0.5\text{ m}\)

subtopic: Vibrations of a Stretched String and Sonometer
stem: A sonometer wire vibrates with frequency \(n_{1}\) in air under suitable load of specific gravity '\(\sigma\)'. When the load is immersed in water, the frequency of vibration of wire \(n_{2}\) will be ________.
solution:
**(B)** \(n_1\sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma - 1}{\sigma}}\)

For a sonometer wire of fixed length and linear density, \(n \propto \sqrt{T}\), so

\(\dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}}\)

In air the tension is the full weight of the load, \(T_1 = V\rho g\), where \(\rho\) is the density of the load.

Immersed in water the load loses weight equal to the weight of water displaced, so

\(T_2 = V\rho g - V\rho_w g = Vg(\rho - \rho_w)\)

Hence

\(\dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\rho - \rho_w}{\rho}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma - 1}{\sigma}}\)

since the specific gravity is \(\sigma = \dfrac{\rho}{\rho_w}\).

\(\therefore n_2 = n_1\sqrt{\dfrac{\sigma - 1}{\sigma}}\)

**Check:** immersion REDUCES the tension, so \(n_2\) must be smaller than \(n_1\). Any expression giving a ratio greater than 1 can therefore be rejected at sight.

stem: Explain analytically how the stationary waves are formed. Hence show that the distance between node and adjacent antinode is \(\frac{\lambda}{4}\) . A set of 48 tuning forks is arranged in a series of descending frequencies such that each fork gives 4 beats per second with the preceding one. The frequency of the first fork is 1.5 times the frequency of the last fork. Find the frequency of the first and \(42^{\text{nd}}\) tuning fork.
solution:
**Formation of a stationary wave**

Let two identical progressive waves travel along the same line in opposite directions:

\(y_1 = A\sin(\omega t - kx)\) and \(y_2 = A\sin(\omega t + kx)\)

By the principle of superposition,

\(y = y_1 + y_2 = A[\sin(\omega t - kx) + \sin(\omega t + kx)]\)

Using \(\sin C + \sin D = 2\sin\dfrac{C+D}{2}\cos\dfrac{C-D}{2}\),

\(y = 2A\cos(kx)\sin(\omega t)\)

This is the equation of a stationary wave. The amplitude \(2A\cos(kx)\) depends on position but not on time, so the wave does not travel.

**Nodes** occur where the amplitude is zero: \(\cos(kx) = 0\), i.e. \(kx = (2p+1)\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), giving

\(x = (2p+1)\dfrac{\lambda}{4} = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}, \dfrac{3\lambda}{4}, \dfrac{5\lambda}{4}, \ldots\)

**Antinodes** occur where the amplitude is maximum: \(\cos(kx) = \pm 1\), i.e. \(kx = p\pi\), giving

\(x = \dfrac{p\lambda}{2} = 0, \dfrac{\lambda}{2}, \lambda, \ldots\)

The distance between a node and the antinode next to it is therefore

\(\dfrac{\lambda}{4} - 0 = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}\)

**Numerical**

The frequencies form an arithmetic progression descending by 4 Hz:

\(n_p = n_1 - 4(p - 1)\)

For the last (48th) fork, \(n_{48} = n_1 - 4(47) = n_1 - 188\).

Given \(n_1 = 1.5\,n_{48}\):

\(n_1 = 1.5(n_1 - 188)\)

\(n_1 = 1.5n_1 - 282\)

\(0.5n_1 = 282\), so \(n_1 = 564\text{ Hz}\)

Check: \(n_{48} = 564 - 188 = 376\text{ Hz}\) and \(\dfrac{564}{376} = 1.5\). 

For the 42nd fork:

\(\therefore n_{42} = 564 - 4(41) = 564 - 164 = 400\text{ Hz}\)

**Frequency of the first fork = 564 Hz; frequency of the 42nd fork = 400 Hz.**

stem: Explain the formation of stationary waves by the analytical method. Show that nodes and antinodes are equally spaced in stationary waves.
solution:
Let two identical progressive waves travel along the same line in opposite directions:

\(y_1 = A\sin(\omega t - kx)\) and \(y_2 = A\sin(\omega t + kx)\)

By the principle of superposition,

\(y = y_1 + y_2 = 2A\cos(kx)\sin(\omega t)\)

using \(\sin C + \sin D = 2\sin\dfrac{C+D}{2}\cos\dfrac{C-D}{2}\).

The amplitude \(2A\cos(kx)\) varies with position only, so the wave does not progress.

**Nodes** (amplitude zero): \(\cos(kx) = 0\), so \(kx = (2p+1)\dfrac{\pi}{2}\) and

\(x = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}, \dfrac{3\lambda}{4}, \dfrac{5\lambda}{4}, \dfrac{7\lambda}{4}, \ldots\)

Successive nodes are separated by \(\dfrac{3\lambda}{4} - \dfrac{\lambda}{4} = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}\).

**Antinodes** (amplitude maximum): \(\cos(kx) = \pm 1\), so \(kx = p\pi\) and

\(x = 0, \dfrac{\lambda}{2}, \lambda, \dfrac{3\lambda}{2}, \ldots\)

Successive antinodes are also separated by \(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\).

Since both sets are spaced \(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\) apart, nodes are equally spaced and antinodes are equally spaced, and each antinode lies exactly midway between two nodes at a distance \(\dfrac{\lambda}{4}\) from each.

stem: Explain the formation of stationary waves by analytical method. Show the formation of stationary wave diagrammatically.
solution:
Let two identical progressive waves travel along the same line in opposite directions:

\(y_1 = A\sin(\omega t - kx)\) and \(y_2 = A\sin(\omega t + kx)\)

By the principle of superposition,

\(y = y_1 + y_2 = A[\sin(\omega t - kx) + \sin(\omega t + kx)]\)

Applying \(\sin C + \sin D = 2\sin\dfrac{C+D}{2}\cos\dfrac{C-D}{2}\),

\(y = 2A\cos(kx)\sin(\omega t)\)

Writing \(R = 2A\cos(kx)\), the result is \(y = R\sin(\omega t)\): every particle performs S.H.M. of the same frequency, but with an amplitude \(R\) that depends on its position \(x\) and not on time. The wave therefore does not travel — it is a STATIONARY wave.

\(R = 0\) where \(\cos(kx) = 0\), giving NODES at \(x = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}, \dfrac{3\lambda}{4}, \dfrac{5\lambda}{4}, \ldots\)

\(R = \pm 2A\) where \(\cos(kx) = \pm 1\), giving ANTINODES at \(x = 0, \dfrac{\lambda}{2}, \lambda, \ldots\)

**Diagrammatic representation**

The formation is shown by plotting the two component waves on a common axis at successive instants \(t = 0,\ \dfrac{T}{4},\ \dfrac{T}{2},\ \dfrac{3T}{4},\ T\), with their resultant below each pair.

At \(t = 0\) the two waves coincide and the resultant has maximum amplitude \(2A\). At \(t = \dfrac{T}{4}\) they are in opposite phase everywhere and the resultant is zero throughout. At \(t = \dfrac{T}{2}\) the resultant again has maximum amplitude but is inverted, and at \(t = T\) the pattern repeats.

In every one of these resultants the same points remain permanently at rest — these are the nodes — while the points midway between them swing with maximum amplitude \(2A\) — these are the antinodes. The pattern only grows and shrinks in place; it does not advance along the medium.

Nodes and antinodes alternate, each node being a distance \(\dfrac{\lambda}{4}\) from the antinode next to it.

stem: Derive an expression for equation of stationary wave on a stretched string. Show that the distance between two successive nodes or antinodes is \(\lambda/2\).
solution:
Consider a progressive wave travelling along a stretched string in the \(+x\) direction and its reflection travelling in the \(-x\) direction:

\(y_1 = A\sin(\omega t - kx)\) and \(y_2 = A\sin(\omega t + kx)\)

By the principle of superposition,

\(y = y_1 + y_2 = A[\sin(\omega t - kx) + \sin(\omega t + kx)]\)

Using \(\sin C + \sin D = 2\sin\dfrac{C+D}{2}\cos\dfrac{C-D}{2}\),

\(y = 2A\cos(kx)\sin(\omega t)\)

This is the equation of the stationary wave, with \(k = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\).

**Successive nodes.** Amplitude is zero where \(\cos(kx) = 0\):

\(\dfrac{2\pi x}{\lambda} = (2p+1)\dfrac{\pi}{2}\), so \(x = (2p+1)\dfrac{\lambda}{4}\)

Taking \(p\) and \(p+1\), the separation of successive nodes is

\(\Delta x = (2p+3)\dfrac{\lambda}{4} - (2p+1)\dfrac{\lambda}{4} = \dfrac{2\lambda}{4} = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}\)

**Successive antinodes.** Amplitude is maximum where \(\cos(kx) = \pm 1\):

\(\dfrac{2\pi x}{\lambda} = p\pi\), so \(x = \dfrac{p\lambda}{2}\)

and the separation of successive antinodes is likewise \(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\).

Hence the distance between two successive nodes, or between two successive antinodes, is \(\dfrac{\lambda}{2}\).

subtopic: Vibrations of a Stretched String and Sonometer
stem: A wire length 1 m and mass 2 g is in unison with a tuning fork of frequency 300 Hz. Calculate the tension produced in the wire.
solution:
The wire vibrates in its fundamental mode in unison with the fork, so \(n = 300\text{ Hz}\).

Linear density:

\(m = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{length}} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-3}}{1} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kg/m}\)

For the fundamental of a stretched wire fixed at both ends,

\(n = \dfrac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{m}}\)

\(300 = \dfrac{1}{2 \times 1}\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{2 \times 10^{-3}}}\)

\(600 = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{2 \times 10^{-3}}}\)

\(3.6 \times 10^{5} = \dfrac{T}{2 \times 10^{-3}}\)

\(\therefore T = 3.6 \times 10^{5} \times 2 \times 10^{-3} = 720\text{ N}\)

**Tension in the wire = 720 N.**

subtopic: Vibrations of a Stretched String and Sonometer
stem: A sonometer wire 1 metre along weighing 2 g is in resonance with a tuning fork of frequency 300 Hz. Find tension in the sonometer wire.
solution:
The wire is in resonance with the fork, so it vibrates in its fundamental mode at \(n = 300\text{ Hz}\).

Linear density:

\(m = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kg}}{1\text{ m}} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kg/m}\)

For the fundamental of a sonometer wire,

\(n = \dfrac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{m}}\)

\(300 = \dfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{2 \times 10^{-3}}}\)

\(600 = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{2 \times 10^{-3}}}\)

\(T = (600)^2 \times 2 \times 10^{-3} = 3.6 \times 10^{5} \times 2 \times 10^{-3}\)

\(\therefore T = 720\text{ N}\)

**Tension in the sonometer wire = 720 N.**

subtopic: Vibrations of a Stretched String and Sonometer
stem: A transverse wave is produced on a stretched string 0.9 m long and fixed at its ends. Find the speed of the transverse wave, when the string vibrates while emitting second overtone of frequency 324 Hz.
solution:
The string is fixed at both ends, so both ends are nodes and ALL harmonics are present.

The second overtone is the THIRD harmonic, for which the string carries 3 loops:

\(L = 3 \times \dfrac{\lambda}{2}\), so \(\lambda = \dfrac{2L}{3} = \dfrac{2 \times 0.9}{3} = 0.6\text{ m}\)

The speed of the transverse wave is

\(\therefore v = n\lambda = 324 \times 0.6 = 194.4\text{ m/s}\)

**Speed of the transverse wave = 194.4 m/s.**

stem: The fundamental frequency of an air column in a pipe closed at one end is in unison with the third overtone of an open pipe. Calculate the ratio of lengths of their air columns.
solution:
Let \(L_c\) be the length of the closed pipe and \(L_o\) that of the open pipe, with the same sound speed \(v\).

**Closed pipe, fundamental:**

\(n_c = \dfrac{v}{4L_c}\)

**Open pipe, third overtone.** An open pipe has all harmonics, so the third overtone is the FOURTH harmonic:

\(n_o = \dfrac{4v}{2L_o} = \dfrac{2v}{L_o}\)

The two are in unison, so \(n_c = n_o\):

\(\dfrac{v}{4L_c} = \dfrac{2v}{L_o}\)

\(L_o = 8L_c\)

\(\therefore \dfrac{L_c}{L_o} = \dfrac{1}{8}\)

**The ratio of the lengths of the air columns (closed : open) is 1 : 8.**

stem: Show that even as well as odd harmonics are present as overtones in the case of an air column vibrating in a pipe open at both ends.
solution:
In a pipe open at both ends, both ends are free, so each end is an ANTINODE with a node between them.

**Fundamental (first harmonic).** One node, two antinodes:

\(L = \dfrac{\lambda_1}{2}\), so \(\lambda_1 = 2L\) and \(n_1 = \dfrac{v}{2L}\)

**First overtone.** Two nodes, three antinodes:

\(L = \lambda_2\), so \(n_2 = \dfrac{v}{L} = 2n_1\)

**Second overtone.** Three nodes, four antinodes:

\(L = \dfrac{3\lambda_3}{2}\), so \(\lambda_3 = \dfrac{2L}{3}\) and \(n_3 = \dfrac{3v}{2L} = 3n_1\)

In general, for \(p\) nodes:

\(n_p = \dfrac{pv}{2L} = p\,n_1\), where \(p = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)

So the frequencies are in the ratio

\(n_1 : n_2 : n_3 : n_4 : \ldots = 1 : 2 : 3 : 4 : \ldots\)

The overtones are the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, ... harmonics — that is, BOTH even harmonics (2nd, 4th, ...) and odd harmonics (3rd, 5th, ...) are present as overtones in a pipe open at both ends.

stem: Show that all harmonics are present in case of an air column vibrating in a pipe open at both ends.
solution:
In a pipe open at both ends, both ends are free to vibrate, so each end is an ANTINODE.

**Fundamental (first harmonic).** The simplest mode has one node at the centre and an antinode at each end:

\(L = \dfrac{\lambda_1}{2}\), so \(\lambda_1 = 2L\) and \(n_1 = \dfrac{v}{\lambda_1} = \dfrac{v}{2L}\)

**First overtone.** Two nodes and three antinodes:

\(L = 2 \times \dfrac{\lambda_2}{2} = \lambda_2\), so \(n_2 = \dfrac{v}{L} = 2n_1\)

**Second overtone.** Three nodes and four antinodes:

\(L = 3 \times \dfrac{\lambda_3}{2}\), so \(\lambda_3 = \dfrac{2L}{3}\) and \(n_3 = \dfrac{3v}{2L} = 3n_1\)

Continuing, with \(p\) nodes in the pipe:

\(n_p = \dfrac{pv}{2L} = p\,n_1\), \(p = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)

Hence

\(n_1 : n_2 : n_3 : \ldots = 1 : 2 : 3 : \ldots\)

Every integral multiple of the fundamental frequency is possible, so ALL harmonics are present in the vibration of an air column in a pipe open at both ends.

stem: Obtain an expression for practical determination of end correction -- (i) for a pipe open at both ends and (ii) for a pipe closed at one end.
solution:
An antinode is not formed exactly at the open end of a pipe but slightly beyond it. This extra distance is called the END CORRECTION \(e\), and it must be added to the measured length of the air column at every open end.

In each case the SAME tuning fork of frequency \(n\) is used for both resonating lengths, so the wavelength \(\lambda = \dfrac{v}{n}\) is the same for both.

**(i) Pipe open at both ends**

Both ends are open, so the correction is applied twice and the effective length is \(L + 2e\).

Let \(L_1\) be the length resonating in the fundamental mode and \(L_2\) the length resonating in the first overtone.

Fundamental: \(L_1 + 2e = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}\), so \(\lambda = 2(L_1 + 2e)\)

First overtone: \(L_2 + 2e = \lambda\)

Equating the two expressions for \(\lambda\),

\(L_2 + 2e = 2(L_1 + 2e)\)

\(L_2 + 2e = 2L_1 + 4e\)

\(L_2 - 2L_1 = 2e\)

\(\therefore e = \dfrac{L_2 - 2L_1}{2}\)

**(ii) Pipe closed at one end**

Only one end is open, so the correction is applied once and the effective length is \(L + e\).

Fundamental: \(L_1 + e = \dfrac{\lambda}{4}\), so \(\lambda = 4(L_1 + e)\)

First overtone (third harmonic): \(L_2 + e = \dfrac{3\lambda}{4}\), so \(\lambda = \dfrac{4(L_2 + e)}{3}\)

Equating the two expressions for \(\lambda\),

\(4(L_1 + e) = \dfrac{4(L_2 + e)}{3}\)

\(3(L_1 + e) = L_2 + e\)

\(3L_1 + 3e = L_2 + e\)

\(L_2 - 3L_1 = 2e\)

\(\therefore e = \dfrac{L_2 - 3L_1}{2}\)

In both cases the end correction is obtained from two measured resonating lengths of the same air column sounded with the same tuning fork.

**\(e = \dfrac{L_2 - 2L_1}{2}\) for a pipe open at both ends, and \(e = \dfrac{L_2 - 3L_1}{2}\) for a pipe closed at one end.**

stem: Two tuning forks have frequencies 450 Hz and 454 Hz respectively. On sounding these forks together, the time interval between two successive maximum intensities will be ________.
solution:
**(A)** \(\dfrac{1}{4}\) s

Successive maxima of intensity are successive beats, so the time between them is the beat period.

Beat frequency:

\(N = n_1 - n_2 = 454 - 450 = 4\text{ Hz}\)

Time interval between two successive maxima:

\(\therefore t = \dfrac{1}{N} = \dfrac{1}{4}\text{ s}\)

stem: Prove that the frequency of beats is equal to the difference between the frequencies of the two sound notes giving rise to beats.
solution:
Let two sound notes of equal amplitude \(A\) and slightly different frequencies \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) (with \(n_1 > n_2\)) reach a point together. Taking both to start in phase,

\(y_1 = A\sin(2\pi n_1 t)\) and \(y_2 = A\sin(2\pi n_2 t)\)

By the principle of superposition,

\(y = y_1 + y_2 = A[\sin(2\pi n_1 t) + \sin(2\pi n_2 t)]\)

Using \(\sin C + \sin D = 2\sin\dfrac{C+D}{2}\cos\dfrac{C-D}{2}\),

\(y = 2A\cos\left[2\pi\left(\dfrac{n_1 - n_2}{2}\right)t\right]\sin\left[2\pi\left(\dfrac{n_1 + n_2}{2}\right)t\right]\)

This is an oscillation of frequency \(\dfrac{n_1 + n_2}{2}\) whose amplitude

\(R = 2A\cos\left[2\pi\left(\dfrac{n_1 - n_2}{2}\right)t\right]\)

varies slowly with time.

The intensity is maximum when \(|\cos(\ldots)| = 1\), i.e. when

\(2\pi\left(\dfrac{n_1 - n_2}{2}\right)t = p\pi\), giving \(t = \dfrac{p}{n_1 - n_2}\), \(p = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\)

So successive maxima occur at times \(0, \dfrac{1}{n_1 - n_2}, \dfrac{2}{n_1 - n_2}, \ldots\)

The interval between two successive maxima is \(\dfrac{1}{n_1 - n_2}\), so the number of maxima per second is

\(N = n_1 - n_2\)

Hence the frequency of beats equals the difference between the frequencies of the two notes.

stem: The wavelengths of two sound waves in air are \(\frac{81}{173}\text{ m}\) and \(\frac{81}{170}\text{ m}\). They produce 10 beats per second. Calculate the velocity of sound in air.
solution:
Let \(v\) be the velocity of sound in air.

\(\lambda_1 = \dfrac{81}{173}\text{ m}\) gives \(n_1 = \dfrac{v}{\lambda_1} = \dfrac{173v}{81}\)

\(\lambda_2 = \dfrac{81}{170}\text{ m}\) gives \(n_2 = \dfrac{v}{\lambda_2} = \dfrac{170v}{81}\)

The shorter wavelength has the higher frequency, so the beat frequency is

\(N = n_1 - n_2 = \dfrac{173v - 170v}{81} = \dfrac{3v}{81}\)

Given \(N = 10\):

\(\dfrac{3v}{81} = 10\)

\(\therefore v = \dfrac{810}{3} = 270\text{ m/s}\)

**Velocity of sound in air = 270 m/s.**

stem: Two sound notes have wavelengths \(\frac{83}{170}\text{ m}\) and \(\frac{83}{172}\text{ m}\) in the air. These notes when sounded together produce 8 beats per second. Calculate the velocity of sound in the air and frequencies of the two notes.
solution:
Let \(v\) be the velocity of sound in air.

\(\lambda_1 = \dfrac{83}{170}\text{ m}\) gives \(n_1 = \dfrac{v}{\lambda_1} = \dfrac{170v}{83}\)

\(\lambda_2 = \dfrac{83}{172}\text{ m}\) gives \(n_2 = \dfrac{v}{\lambda_2} = \dfrac{172v}{83}\)

The shorter wavelength has the higher frequency, so the beat frequency is

\(N = n_2 - n_1 = \dfrac{172v - 170v}{83} = \dfrac{2v}{83}\)

Given \(N = 8\):

\(\dfrac{2v}{83} = 8\)

\(\therefore v = \dfrac{8 \times 83}{2} = 332\text{ m/s}\)

The two frequencies are then

\(n_1 = \dfrac{170 \times 332}{83} = 680\text{ Hz}\)

\(n_2 = \dfrac{172 \times 332}{83} = 688\text{ Hz}\)

Check: \(688 - 680 = 8\) beats per second, as given.

**Velocity of sound = 332 m/s; the frequencies are 680 Hz and 688 Hz.**

stem: Two tuning forks of frequencies 320 Hz and 340 Hz are sounded together to produce sound wave. The velocity of sound in air is 326.4 m/s. Calculate the difference in wavelengths of these waves.
solution:
Using \(\lambda = \dfrac{v}{n}\) with \(v = 326.4\text{ m/s}\):

\(\lambda_1 = \dfrac{326.4}{320} = 1.02\text{ m}\)

\(\lambda_2 = \dfrac{326.4}{340} = 0.96\text{ m}\)

Difference in wavelengths:

\(\therefore \lambda_1 - \lambda_2 = 1.02 - 0.96 = 0.06\text{ m}\)

**The difference in wavelength is 0.06 m (6 cm).**

stem: Two tuning forks having frequencies 320 Hz and 340 Hz are sounded together to produce sound waves. The velocity of sound in air is 340 m/s. Find the difference in wavelength of these waves.
solution:
Using \(\lambda = \dfrac{v}{n}\) with \(v = 340\text{ m/s}\):

\(\lambda_1 = \dfrac{340}{320} = 1.0625\text{ m}\)

\(\lambda_2 = \dfrac{340}{340} = 1\text{ m}\)

Difference in wavelengths:

\(\therefore \lambda_1 - \lambda_2 = 1.0625 - 1 = 0.0625\text{ m}\)

**The difference in wavelength is 0.0625 m (6.25 cm).**

stem: A stretched sonometer wire is in unison with a tuning fork. When the length of the wire is increased by 5%, the number of beats heard per second is 10. Find the frequency of the tuning fork.
solution:
Let \(n\) be the frequency of the tuning fork and \(L\) the original vibrating length of the wire.

Initially the wire is in unison with the fork, so its frequency is also \(n\).

For a sonometer wire under fixed tension, \(n \propto \dfrac{1}{L}\).

When the length is increased by 5%, the new length is \(L' = 1.05L\) and the new frequency is

\(n' = n \times \dfrac{L}{L'} = \dfrac{n}{1.05}\)

The beat frequency is the difference:

\(n - n' = n - \dfrac{n}{1.05} = n\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{1.05}\right) = n \times \dfrac{0.05}{1.05} = \dfrac{n}{21}\)

Given that 10 beats per second are heard:

\(\dfrac{n}{21} = 10\)

\(\therefore n = 210\text{ Hz}\)

**Frequency of the tuning fork = 210 Hz.**

stem: What is meant by harmonics? Show that only odd harmonics are present as overtones in the case of an air column vibrating in a pipe closed at one end.
solution:
**Harmonics**

The harmonics are the frequencies that are integral multiples of the fundamental frequency. The fundamental itself is the first harmonic; twice the fundamental is the second harmonic, and so on. An OVERTONE is any tone of frequency higher than the fundamental that is actually produced by the given vibrating system, numbered in order of increasing frequency.

**Pipe closed at one end**

The closed end must be a NODE and the open end an ANTINODE.

**Fundamental (first harmonic).** One node and one antinode:

\(L = \dfrac{\lambda_1}{4}\), so \(\lambda_1 = 4L\) and \(n_1 = \dfrac{v}{4L}\)

**First overtone.** Two nodes and two antinodes:

\(L = \dfrac{3\lambda_2}{4}\), so \(\lambda_2 = \dfrac{4L}{3}\) and \(n_2 = \dfrac{3v}{4L} = 3n_1\)

**Second overtone.** Three nodes and three antinodes:

\(L = \dfrac{5\lambda_3}{4}\), so \(\lambda_3 = \dfrac{4L}{5}\) and \(n_3 = \dfrac{5v}{4L} = 5n_1\)

In general, for \(p\) nodes:

\(n_p = \dfrac{(2p-1)v}{4L} = (2p-1)n_1\), \(p = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)

So the frequencies are in the ratio

\(n_1 : n_2 : n_3 : \ldots = 1 : 3 : 5 : \ldots\)

Only ODD multiples of the fundamental are possible. Hence only odd harmonics are present as overtones in an air column vibrating in a pipe closed at one end; the even harmonics are absent.

stem: What are harmonics and overtones (Two points)?
solution:
**Harmonics**

The harmonics are the frequencies that are integral multiples of the fundamental frequency of a vibrating body. The fundamental frequency itself is called the first harmonic.

**Overtones**

The overtones are the tones of frequency HIGHER than the fundamental that are actually produced by the given vibrating body, numbered in ascending order of frequency: the first overtone is the next possible frequency above the fundamental, and so on.

**Two points of distinction**

1. Every integral multiple of the fundamental is a harmonic, whether or not the body can produce it; an overtone is a frequency the body ACTUALLY produces.
2. The harmonics form a complete series \(n, 2n, 3n, \ldots\), whereas which of them appear as overtones depends on the system. In a pipe open at both ends all harmonics appear, so the first overtone is the second harmonic; in a pipe closed at one end only odd harmonics appear, so the first overtone is the THIRD harmonic.

stem: Explain harmonics and overtones.
solution:
**Harmonics**

The harmonics of a vibrating body are the frequencies that are integral multiples of its fundamental frequency \(n\), namely \(n, 2n, 3n, 4n, \ldots\) The fundamental frequency itself is the first harmonic, \(2n\) is the second harmonic, and so on.

**Overtones**

The overtones are those tones, of frequency greater than the fundamental, that the body is actually able to produce. They are numbered in increasing order of frequency — the first overtone is the lowest frequency above the fundamental that the body emits.

**Relation between the two**

Which harmonics appear as overtones depends on the vibrating system.

- Stretched string fixed at both ends, or a pipe open at both ends: all harmonics are present, so

  \(n_1 : n_2 : n_3 : \ldots = 1 : 2 : 3 : \ldots\)

  and the first overtone is the second harmonic.

- Pipe closed at one end: only odd harmonics are present, so

  \(n_1 : n_2 : n_3 : \ldots = 1 : 3 : 5 : \ldots\)

  and the first overtone is the third harmonic.

So every overtone is a harmonic, but not every harmonic is necessarily produced as an overtone.
